note.text: Deductive reasoning aims at a conclusion guaranteed by its premises when the form is valid. Inductive reasoning offers support of a degree: a larger, more representative sample can improve it without making the conclusion certain. Symbolic logic represents relationships with signs; informal analysis examines arguments in ordinary language. Symbolic and informal are ways of presenting or examining reasoning, not synonyms for deductive and inductive. A claim can be symbolised without becoming true.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: Deductive reasoning aims at a conclusion guaranteed by its premises when the form is valid. Inductive reasoning offers support of a degree: a larger, more representative sample can improve it without making the conclusion certain. Symbolic logic represents relationships with signs; informal analysis examines arguments in ordinary language. Symbolic and informal are ways of presenting or examining reasoning, not synonyms for deductive and inductive. A claim can be symbolised without becoming true.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: Ayuk checks a club rule that applies to every member and then applies it to a named member: this can be a deduction. Ngozi samples several market stalls to estimate a wider pattern: this is induction. Either argument can be written in ordinary sentences, and some relationships can also be represented symbolically.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Identify the kind of support being claimed. For a deduction, try to imagine true premises with a false conclusion. For an induction, ask about sample size, selection and alternative explanations. Do not mistake a sequence of impressive symbols for reliable evidence.
